extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, researchers, and readers concerned with peer review integrity
extracted.subtask_description: A news-coverage compilation of cases and signals of compromised or problematic peer review across journals, showing what practices and red flags lead to investigations and retractions. Useful for understanding standards and failure modes in peer review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromised peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the peer review process for an article or issue was 'compromised' (e.g., rigged, manipulated, or not independently conducted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: multiple articles retracted after publisher investigations found compromised review; used as a grounds for mass retraction when integrity cannot be restored. Signals include unusually homogeneous reviewer lists, unexplained rapid acceptances, or reviewer identities that cannot be verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest editor selecting reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Guest editors selecting the peer reviewers for a special issue (rather than the journal editorial office) can create conflicts and vulnerabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a guest editor selected reviewers who were largely affiliated with a single institution and the guest editor was not named in the issue — this contributed to a finding of compromised review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of reviewer affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: A majority of reviewers being affiliated with the same institution (or small set of institutions) is a red flag for biased or non-independent review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction Watch reports instances where most reviewers were affiliated with one university (e.g., Nanjing University), prompting investigations and retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular patterns in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Unusual or irregular patterns in reviewer assignments, timing, or reports that suggest manipulation or fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendors or platform monitoring can detect irregularities across submissions/special issues (e.g., repeated reviewer selections, identical review text, unnatural timing), which may trigger publisher investigations and mass retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review rings / self-peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups of authors/reviewers who conspire to review each other's work positively (peer review rings) or authors reviewing their own work under false identities (self-peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author-recommended reviewer lists have historically enabled such rings; journals may remove author-suggested reviewers to reduce this risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest from author-suggested reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing authors to suggest reviewers can create conflicts of interest when suggested reviewers are mentors, colleagues, or otherwise likely to provide favorable reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cureus halted author-suggested reviewers due to potential conflicts and their role in enabling peer review rings and biased positive feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient verification via institutional email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Using institutional email addresses alone to verify reviewer/author identity is no longer a reliable safeguard, as bad actors can obtain or spoof 'round-trip-verified' institutional emails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: OpenReview analysis found fake reviewer profiles using round-trip-verified addresses from reputed universities; publishers should augment email verification with other checks (ORCID, institutional confirmation, known researcher profiles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake reviewer identities / profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer profiles that are fabricated or impersonated, undermining the authenticity of reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OpenReview staff found dozens of fake reviewer profiles at AI conferences; such profiles can be used to accept low-quality work or bypass genuine peer evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment or inducement to editors ('article brokers')
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party brokers offering to pay editors or provide 'expedited processing' for a fee, creating a financial conflict of interest and undermining editorial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: emails offering $500–$1,000 per accepted manuscript to 'support the review process' were used to try to influence editors — journals should monitor for and prohibit such arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technobabble / lack of substantive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts that appear to be full of jargon or irrelevant technical content, lacking a clear gist, meaningful figures, or coherent methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: irrelevant MATLAB functions, figures that don't depict the claimed anatomy (sine wave passed off as anatomical structure), and discussions that read like literature reviews rather than engagement with results — reviewers should assess clarity, relevance, and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient data or methodological support for claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a manuscript are not supported by the data or methods presented (e.g., imaging resolution too low to visualize the claimed structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reviewer questioned whether publicly available MRI resolution was sufficient to visualize the indusium griseum; reviewers should check that data quality and methods support conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequate or irrelevant figures and code
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures, code, or supplementary materials that are irrelevant to the manuscript's claims or fail to support the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances where provided MATLAB functions were irrelevant or figures did not match described anatomy highlight the need for reviewers to scrutinize supporting materials for relevance and correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship irregularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems with authorship attribution, contribution statements, or ghost/guest authorship that raise concerns about the integrity of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions have followed investigations that flagged authorship issues alongside peer review irregularities; journals should verify authorship and contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblower or external flagging as trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports from whistleblowers, readers, or external parties can reveal irregularities that prompt formal investigations into review or authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a whistleblower flagged irregularities leading to multiple retractions; publishers should have procedures to evaluate and respond to credible external reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-publication review may be initiated when issues are raised about research methodology, conclusions, or conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: expression of concern and post-publication peer review conducted when methodology, conclusions, or author COIs were questioned; such reviews can lead to corrections or retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced vetting of guest editors and reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should implement tighter vetting processes for guest editors and peer reviewers to prevent compromised review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers enhanced vetting after investigations that led to the retraction of dozens or hundreds of articles; vetting can include identity verification, conflict checks, and limits on guest editor control of reviewer selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher governance and editorial-process transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to editorial processes (e.g., implementing multiple reviews or removing editors) should be transparent and consider disciplinary norms to avoid diluting review quality or provoking resignations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: mathematics editors resigned after a publisher unilaterally required more reviewers; disciplines with line-by-line correctness checks may be harmed by processes that ignore workload and quality trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring via vendors and platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party vendors or submission platforms can monitor for anomalous patterns and alert publishers to potential problems in peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: an ASTM vendor noticed irregular patterns that prompted an investigation; publishers should use monitoring tools and follow up on vendor alerts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recommendation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer recommendations coming from authors are empirically more likely to yield positive feedback and therefore can bias editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may restrict or eliminate author-suggested reviewers to reduce this bias, as some publishers have done in response to detected abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass retraction as remediation for irreparably compromised review
rubrics_metrics.description: When the peer review process is found to be irreparably compromised across multiple articles or an issue, journals may retract affected papers en masse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: special issues and sections where investigations found compromised reviews resulted in retraction of dozens to hundreds of papers; retraction notices often document the compromised process and rationale.
